output.briefing:
Focus on the assigned exceptional anchor pair {-1,1}; do not conflate it with the same-sign integer-anchor case. If two integer elements have opposite signs, the supplied L1 argument forces their product to be -1, hence they are {-1,1}. For any other element x, the anchor conditions make 1+x and 1-x rational squares, so -1≤x≤1. The endpoints are the anchors, and the only integer strictly between them is 0, forbidden as an element. Thus all four remaining elements in this case must be noninteger rationals in (-1,1). This reduction does not imply they are positive.

Here is an exact common-neighbor parametrization to develop. Write p²=1+x and q²=1-x. Then p²+q²=2 and x=(p²-q²)/2. The rational points on this conic are parametrized by lines q=1+t(p-1) through (1,1): solving gives p=(t²-2t-1)/(t²+1), q=(1-2t-t²)/(t²+1), and therefore x=f(t)=4t(1-t²)/(1+t²)² for t∈Q. The omitted vertical-line point (p,q)=(1,-1) also gives x=0; it creates no missing nonzero common neighbor. Conversely the conic parametrization shows every nonzero rational common neighbor occurs as f(t). The zero values t=0,±1 are degenerate and should be excluded when parametrizing nonzero elements. Check the derivation and converse explicitly in the final proof; the parameter is not necessarily unique for x.

For the proposed symmetric set {1,-1,u,-u,v,-v}, the six conditions 1+u, 1-u, 1+v, 1-v, 1+uv, 1-uv ∈ Q² are sufficient as well as necessary, provided the elements are nonzero and pairwise distinct. Indeed the six conditions give anchor-to-element and cross-pair conditions; moreover (1+u)(1-u)=1-u² and (1+v)(1-v)=1-v² are rational squares, supplying the two within-opposite-pair conditions. Equivalently, with C={x∈Q:1+x,1-x∈Q²}, the criterion is u,v,uv∈C, together with u,v≠0 and u≠±v. The restrictions u,v∈C already rule out u or v equal to ±1. Verify all pair classes to avoid overlooking a pair. Substituting u=f(r), v=f(s), uv=f(w) yields an explicit rational parameter constraint to investigate; it is a reduction, not evidence that a nondegenerate solution exists or that the resulting curve has a rational point.

The preferred direction is a genuine contradiction argument, but no proof method is mandated. A possible route is to analyze the rational parameter constraint for u,v,uv∈C, including its exceptional/degenerate components, and seek a descent or arithmetic obstruction; alternatively seek an exact nondegenerate rational point and verify all fifteen pairs. Do not claim global nonexistence from bounded search or infer existence from the six square conditions without checking distinctness and nonzero elements. Supplied prior work L1 and L2 is relevant background, but no reusable lemma IDs, attempt IDs, or review IDs are available in this snapshot. The supplied evidence does not settle this exceptional case or the main problem. Prior finite searches are bounded/mechanism-specific and were not independently rerun here; cited external literature and locators were not externally verified.
uncertainties: No exact nondegenerate symmetric sextuple or obstruction to one is supplied; the rational-point question for u,v,uv∈C remains open in this briefing.
The prior finite computation counts and fingerprint were not independently validated from the supplied artifacts, and cannot establish an unbounded-height result.
The cited external references and locators in the supplied notes remain unverified; use only the displayed algebra as supplied context, not as independently checked external authority.

assumptions: All six elements belong to Q and are nonzero.
All six elements are pairwise distinct.
At least two elements belong to Z.
For each of the fifteen unordered pairs, the product plus 1 belongs to Q squared; a zero square root is allowed.
quantifiers: Existentially over six pairwise distinct nonzero rational numbers.
At least two of those six numbers are integers.
Universally over all fifteen unordered pairs.
Any nonexistence conclusion must cover unbounded rational height and every allowable integer pair.
problem_contract.statement: Determine whether there exists a set S of six pairwise distinct nonzero rational numbers such that at least two elements are integers and xy+1 is a rational square for every two distinct x,y in S. Track the all-positive case separately from the unrestricted-sign case. Give an exact valid example or an unrestricted nonexistence proof; otherwise record only explicitly scoped partial results.
